articles.title: Every generation had its own Dolly Parton
articles.summary: From "Jolene" and Miley Cyrus to Dollywood and the Imagination Library, Dolly Parton gave every generation a way to call her their own.
articles.body:
When news broke yesterday that Dolly Parton had died , one of the first people I thought of was my friend's 8-year-old daughter. To her, Parton wasn't simply a country star from her parents' generation. She was one of her own heroes.

The girl had recently chosen Parton for a major school project about changemakers: people who had made a positive contribution to the world. She loved Parton's music, but what impressed her most was the Imagination Library and the millions of books Parton had provided to children. Her fascination even helped inspire the family's summer trip to Dollywood.

Then my 71-year-old dad texted me about how sad he was.

"Everybody — and I mean every one of us — loved her," he wrote. "Who else has done that? Particularly in these times. We are all mourning this one. It hits hard."

He and my friend's daughter are separated by more than six decades and discovered Parton in completely different ways. Yet somehow, the superstar belonged equally to both of them.

In Metairie, La., 7-year-old Elsie Novak marked the loss in her own way. After hearing the news, she dressed in head-to-toe pink — complete with a cowboy hat and boots — pulled out her pink guitar and paid tribute to Dolly .

That was Parton's rarest kind of staying power. She didn't simply retain the fans who grew up alongside her. Across eight decades, she kept creating new ways for people to find her.

For some, the doorway was "Jolene." For others, it was 9 to 5 , Whitney Houston's version of "I Will Always Love You" or Miley Cyrus calling her "Aunt Dolly" on Hannah Montana . Children met her through Dollywood, an Imagination Library book, a pandemic bedtime story or even — as my own 7-year-old daughter did three years ago — a brightly colored Gap T-shirt.

There was always another doorway into Dolly.

Parton first entered American homes in the 1960s through The Porter Wagoner Show . By the end of the following decade, she had crossed beyond country music with songs including "Here You Come Again." Then came the blockbuster film 9 to 5 and its chart-topping theme song, followed by The Best Little Whorehouse in Texas , "Islands in the Stream" with Kenny Rogers and Steel Magnolias .

She became a star people could grow up alongside, but she never became trapped in the era that first made her famous.

Yahoo writer Dana Yewbank discovered Parton as an "awkward teenager" fumbling her way through learning to play guitar. She doesn't remember where she first heard "Jolene," but she remembers what it did to her.

"'Jolene' really grabbed me and planted me on a particular musical path," Yewbank says. "There are very few songs that have affected me that much."

After learning to play the tune, she performed it "ad nauseam" at open mic nights in her town. Her mother still asks her to play it whenever she picks up a guitar.

"I was already a singer — a choir kid — but that song really helped me find my own voice and sensibility within folk and country music," she says.

Of course, there is also a simpler explanation for the song's reach.

"It's just such an absolute banger," Yewbank bluntly (and accurately) puts it.

The riff is addictive, the story immediate and the desperation in Parton's voice as urgent now as it was when "Jolene" was released in 1974. Artists across genres have continually reinterpreted it, giving new listeners a doorway into Parton's music.

One of those artists was Miley Cyrus , who did more than bring "Jolene" to her own fans: She became Parton's clearest bridge to a younger generation.

Parton appeared as Aunt Dolly on Disney Channel's Hannah Montana , mirroring her real-life role as Cyrus's godmother. Cyrus, in turn, made "Jolene" part of her own performances and introduced Parton to viewers who hadn't been alive for her biggest country and pop hits.

Parton understood exactly what that relationship had done for her career. "You really introduced me to a whole new set of fans, young ones," Parton told Cyrus . (Young fans mourning Parton this week confirmed as much: "The first time I ever saw Dolly Parton was on [the] Hannah Montana series, and I have loved her ever since," one fan posted on X .)

That connection was more than a famous friend lending credibility to a Disney show. Parton and Cyrus seemed to recognize something in each other: the huge voices, the exaggerated images and the refusal to let others decide who they should be. As Cyrus grew up, their relationship allowed fans to grow with both of them.

Parton also created a connection with children that didn't depend on their parents' musical tastes.

She founded Dolly Parton's Imagination Library in 1995, inspired by her father, who never learned to read or write. What began as a program sending books to children in her East Tennessee home county grew into an international literacy initiative. It has now distributed more than 300 million free books to children from birth to age 5 and sends more than 3 million books each month, according to the organization .

Some children took that relationship literally. An Indiana preschooler, Hallie Day, began carrying a picture of Parton everywhere she went and calling the singer her "best friend." Her family's affection for Parton began with the Imagination Library: Whenever a new book arrived, her mother would tell the children it was "from Dolly."

After going viral on TikTok last year, Hallie's mother told People her daughter eventually fell in love with the music too, particularly "Coat of Many Colors." But Parton represented something larger to her. "She inspires Hallie to be loud, bubbly and completely herself ," she said. "I couldn't ask for a better role model for my daughter."

To many of those children, Parton was simply "the Book Lady," a title she once said meant more to her than being called the queen of country music.

"I love to sing, I love to write, but I have loved doing this for the kids," she said on Today . "There's nothing more important than our little kids, to make an impression on them when they're young and to teach them the right things early on."

During the pandemic, that mission took on a new form. In April 2020, as families faced isolation and uncertainty, Parton launched Goodnight With Dolly , a 10-week online series in which she read children's books from bed. She began with The Little Engine That Could and said she wanted "to share a story and to share some love." The series remains available through the Imagination Library .

That was how Yahoo editor Erin Donnelly's then-toddler son Beau discovered her. To children like him, Parton wasn't a legacy performer being introduced through an old song or movie. She was a comforting presence who showed up at bedtime during a frightening and confusing moment in their childhood.

Other children encountered Parton through books of a different kind. My Little Golden Book About Dolly Parton , released in 2021, turned her life into a story for readers ages 4 to 8, tracing her journey from a childhood in rural Tennessee to becoming a singer, songwriter, actor, philanthropist and cultural icon. A board book edition now introduces that story to babies.

Then there are the less profound — but no less real — introductions.

My daughter Jolie recognized Dolly because of a Gap T-shirt. She didn't know "Coat of Many Colors" or understand the significance of the woman smiling on the front. She simply loved the colors. Then we started playing her music.

A T-shirt may be a superficial doorway, but it is still a doorway. Children often meet an icon through an image before they know the work or the history behind it. Dolly, with the towering hair, rhinestones and bright colors, was instantly recognizable even to people who couldn't name one of her songs.

By the time my friend and her family arrived at Dollywood this summer, the daughter who had done her school project on Parton already understood that Dolly was more than a famous face.

They saw families spanning generations and a park where music and Smoky Mountain traditions mattered as much as the roller coasters. Parton's relatives performed there. The family was also struck by how varied and, in her experience, welcoming the crowd felt.

Dollywood opened in Pigeon Forge, Tenn., in 1986. Four decades later, the theme park and Parton's affiliated East Tennessee businesses attract more than 4 million visitors annually and have created thousands of jobs and opportunities in the region, according to Parton's official biography .

The girl who had studied Dolly's charitable work in a classroom could now see what it looked like for someone to reinvest in the place that raised her.

That may be why Parton moved so easily across generations. Her image was larger than life, but her impact was tangible: She was a glittering movie star who could also put a book in a child's hands. She never chased younger audiences by disguising her age or sanding away what made her distinctive. She simply kept creating new ways for people to find her.

Her rarest gift may have been ensuring that no generation had to borrow Dolly from the one before it. She gave each one a Dolly of its own.

articles.title: Quote of the day by Christopher Walken: ‘We're born alone. We die alone. And in between, we spend our lives looking for connection…’, when the ‘Pulp Fiction’ star shared words of wisdom highlighting how the true meaning of life stems from true friendship
articles.summary: Explore Christopher Walken's insightful quote about the importance of true friendship and human connection, shared while filming a commercial. The veteran actor reflects on life's ultimate pursuit of meaningful relationships.
articles.body: Christopher Walken is a veteran face in the industry who has had his own set of highs and lows in life. Working in an industry where you have to be on your toes at all times, the actor learned the meaning of true friendship over the years. Today’s quote resonates with his experience over the years of understanding that good friends and connections are the only ones that stay with you in the long run. Some people only stay for a short time and then leave; however, there are those few friends who stay by your side—friends the actor believes you must always hold onto.What the quote of the day reads: “We're born alone. We die alone. And in between, we spend our lives looking for something: connection. That's all we want. Every once in a while, we might find it in a true friend. Many friendships will come only to fade as quickly as a firework, but some, a rare and precious few, turn life up to 11 and keep it there. You have to hold on to friends like these because, just like air, you'll miss them when they're gone.”What does the quote mean?Christopher Walken shared these words of wisdom with the world while filming a commercial for a popular German mountain bike brand. The ad, which Walken was a part of, was directed by Phil Hawkins.The quote is essentially talking about the grounding reality that life begins on its own and ends on its own. Ultimately, the individual human connections we make in between are what make everything worthwhile. Oftentimes, the search for meaningful connection becomes our primary emotional drive in everyday life. He emphasises holding onto people who support you through thick and thin; these are the people you need by your side at all times.Most relationships are temporary, bright, and brief like fireworks. However, a few relationships amplify our experience of the world and enrich our lives to the point where we can happily move forward every day because there is someone to look forward to. Walken puts the utmost importance on human relationships and how they are one of the most important things and main necessities of life if you need to survive.By comparing deep friendships to air, the quote frames true companionship not as a form of luxury or a social preference, but as an essential element for survival. We take bonds and people close to us for granted until their absence leaves us in isolation.About Christopher Walken’s lifeChristopher Walken is perhaps one of the most influential and iconic figures in the Hollywood industry. He was born to the name Ronald Walken on March 31, 1943, in New York City. Later in life, he adopted the stage name Christopher and started working in the entertainment industry. Walken was heavily interested in acting and trained in dance and musical theatre from a young age. He also began working in the entertainment industry as a child actor for live television shows during the 1950s. Not only that, but he also dabbled in Broadway from a young age.He worked on a lot of projects; however, his big break came with ‘Annie Hall’ (1977). Later on, he appeared in ‘The Deer Hunter’ (1978), which helped him earn his first-ever Academy Award for Best Supporting Actor for his powerful performance. Some of his other popular roles over the years include ‘The Dogs of War’ (1980), The ‘Dead Zone’ (1983), the ‘James Bond’ film ‘A View to a Kill’ (1985), ‘Pulp Fiction’ (1994), ‘Catch Me If You Can’ (2002), and ‘Dune: Part Two’ (2024).Christopher Walken's upcoming projectChristopher Walken will next appear in the dark comedy film ‘Back in Black’, which is scheduled to premiere on September 13, 2026. The plot revolves around a small-town funeral director, Clyde Mortimer, who is going out of business because apparently the place has witnessed a wave of wellness craze, and people are just not dying like they used to. His granddaughter Sam, who will be played by Ella Ballentine, decides to do something on her own to help her family's business, no matter the cost. The movie features a stellar cast, including stars like Jane Curtin, Deborah Grover, Stuart Hughes, Watson Rose, Russell Yuen, Mary Ashton, Louise Lambert, Tom Keat, Angelica Alejandro, Sandra Flores, Giamo Alfredi, Christian Laurin and Carl Hines.Give your child the gift of confidence! articles.title: Zé Maria, ex-presidente do Colo-Colo, aos 72 anos na Bahia | G1
articles.standfirst: Ex-dirigente do time de Ilhéus faleceu neste domingo (30), na cidade. José Maria Almeida de Santana era reconhecido também por seu trabalho como comunicador.
articles.summary: Ex-dirigente do time de Ilhéus faleceu neste domingo (30), na cidade. José Maria Almeida de Santana era reconhecido também por seu trabalho como comunicador.
articles.body:
Morre Zé Maria, ex-presidente do Colo-Colo-, aos 72 anos — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

O desportista, jornalista e radialista José Maria Almeida de Santana morreu neste domingo (30), aos 72 anos, em Ilhéus , no sul da Bahia. Zé Maria , como era mais conhecido, é lembrado como "eterno presidente" do Colo-Colo de Futebol e Regatas , time da cidade que conquistou suas maiores glórias quando comandado pelo dirigente.

Conforme apurado pela TV Santa Cruz, afiliada da TV Bahia na região, ele sofreu um infarto agudo do miocárdio e não resistiu.

O desportista esteve à frente do Colo-Colo entre 1992 e 2011. No ano de 2006, o clube venceu o Campeonato Baiano da Série A.

Ao lamentar a morte do ex-dirigente nas redes sociais, o time relembrou a trajetória dele:

"Zé Maria assumiu o Tigre ainda em um período de futebol amador e foi responsável por conduzir o clube ao profissionalismo, disputando e conquistando o título da Série B do Campeonato Baiano em 1999. Sob seu comando, o Colo-Colo permaneceu por 12 anos consecutivos na primeira divisão estadual", elencou alguns feitos.

O ex-dirigente se destacou também como comentarista e comunicador. Em nota, a Associação Baiana de Imprensa (ABI) destacou que ele foi um dos fundadores da Regional Sul da entidade na região, além de colunista em diversos jornais regionais e criador do Troféu Imprensa do Sul da Bahia.

Como ressaltou a ABI, Zé Maria seguia na ativa como comentarista esportivo no programa Gabriela Esportiva, da rádio Gabriela FM, em Ilhéus.

"Nesse momento de tristeza e dor, externamos nossa solidariedade aos familiares, amigos e colegas da imprensa e da crônica esportiva", disse a ABI.

Colo-Colo manifestou pesar pela morte de seu 'eterno presidente' — Foto: Reprodução/Redes Sociais

A Prefeitura de Ilhéus se manifestou com a publicação de um decreto de luto oficial no município. Válida por três dias, a medida leva em conta os anos de dedicação e amor destinados pelo comunicador ao esporte, seu pioneirismo e dinamismo cultural e o "feito histórico que colocou Ilhéus no ápice do futebol estadual", entre outros destaques da carreira.

O velório de Zé Maria ocorre nesta tarde, na SAF, no bairro Conquista, conforme divulgado pelo Colo-Colo no Instagram. O sepultamento será na manhã de segunda-feira (31), no Cemitério do Pontal.

articles.title: Trabalhador que morreu ao cair de alegoria do Festival de Cirandas de Manacapuru é velado no Amazonas | G1
articles.standfirst: Jone Salgado, de 45 anos, fazia parte da equipe responsável pela confecção das alegorias da Ciranda Flor Matizada. Velório ocorreu em Parintins.
articles.summary: Jone Salgado, de 45 anos, fazia parte da equipe responsável pela confecção das alegorias da Ciranda Flor Matizada. Velório ocorreu em Parintins.
articles.body:
O corpo do montador alegórico Jone Salgado foi velado neste domingo (30), por familiares e amigos, que prestaram as últimas homenagens e se despediram do artista.

Familiares, amigos e integrantes do meio cultural se reuniram na Funerária Bentes para a última despedida ao artista, marcada pela emoção e pelas homenagens à trajetória.

Jone Salgado tinha 45 anos, era montador alegórico e fazia parte da equipe responsável pela confecção das alegorias da Ciranda Flor Matizada, uma das agremiações que participam do Festival de Cirandas de Manacapuru , no interior do Amazonas.

O trabalhador fazia parte de uma equipe de profissionais que veio de Parintins para trabalhar na confecção e montagem das alegorias da ciranda para o festival deste ano, que iniciou na sexta.

Jone Salgado, de 45 anos, vítima de queda de alegoria durante montagem para Festival de Cirandas em Manacapuru. — Foto: Arquivo Pessoal

O acidente aconteceu na sexta-feira (28), na Arena Parque do Ingá, onde estavam sendo realizadas as montagens das alegorias para o Festival de Cirandas de Manacapuru.

Segundo informações de trabalhadores que estavam no local, Jone trabalhava dentro de um módulo alegórico e fazia a soldagem da cabeça de um dos bonecos. Após terminar o serviço, ele começou a descer pela estrutura.

Durante a descida, ele precisou trocar o equipamento de segurança. Jhone teria retirado o cinto que utilizava e, antes de conseguir recolocar o equipamento, escorregou ao se aproximar da base da alegoria.

Ainda conforme os relatos, ele pisou em uma área revestida por pano, perdeu o equilíbrio e caiu no solo. A queda ocorreu de uma altura estimada em 12 metros.

Jone foi socorrido e levado ao Hospital Regional de Manacapuru — Lázaro Reis, mas não resistiu aos ferimentos.

A Ciranda Flor Matizada lamentou a morte e afirmou que o artista deixou sua marca na história da ciranda e no coração de cada torcedor.

Morte ocorreu exatos quatro anos de outro acidente fatal no local

O acidente desta sexta-feira aconteceu exatamente quatro anos após outra tragédia durante o Festival de Cirandas de Manacapuru.

Em 28 de agosto de 2022, durante o 22º Festival de Cirandas, uma alegoria da Ciranda Flor Matizada que estava suspensa se desprendeu de um guindaste e caiu. A autônoma Vivian Ramos da Silva morreu e outras 25 pessoas ficaram feridas.

Na época, diversas vítimas foram internadas em unidades de saúde do Amazonas, algumas em estado grave. Vivian e os feridos eram integrantes da ciranda e participavam da apresentação no momento da tragédia.

O caso foi investigado pela Polícia Civil e, em 2023, a Justiça determinou que um técnico que despencou do guindaste recebesse R$ 70 mil de indenização.

articles.title: Rajkumar Santoshi disagrees with Shabana Azmi over Sunny Deol's muslim character in ‘Batwara 1947’; 'Amitabh Bachchan played Muslim hero in ‘Coolie'
articles.summary: ‘Batwara 1947’, one of the year's most eagerly awaited releases starring Sunny Deol, ended up with a mixed critical reception and a disappointing run .
articles.body: ‘Batwara 1947’, one of the year's most eagerly awaited releases starring Sunny Deol, ended up with a mixed critical reception and a disappointing run at the box office. Shabana Azmi recently weighed in on the film's underperformance, suggesting that many audiences struggled to accept Sunny Deol as a Muslim character since it didn't fit his familiar "action patriot" image. Now, director Rajkumar Santoshi has also responded to her recent remarks with clarity.Rajkumar Santoshi on ‘Batwara 1947’In an interview with Variety India, Rajkumar dismissed Shabana's theory, pointing out that even a superstar like Amitabh Bachchan has played Muslim characters in the past, citing his role in Coolie and the several Manmohan Desai films that featured Muslim heroes. He questioned, “It makes no sense to me. Amitabh Bachchan played a Muslim hero in ‘Coolie.’ So many of Manmohan Desai’s films had Muslim heroes. Are we at a point where we cannot accept a hero from the other community? We are sensible, good people, educated people. How are they saying there’s a big mistake in the film?”.In the same conversation, Rajkumar admitted that society today has grown noticeably more rigid and closed-minded. Reflecting on his 2001 film ‘Lajja’ and whether its segment drawing on the ‘Ramayana’ would find acceptance with contemporary audiences, he remarked, “We have become far less tolerant and inclusive as a people. You should look at the filmmaker’s intent and what the writer wants to say. I’m a Hindu. I go to the temple. My son’s name is Ram. I am not against any faith. But I want to take the best of every faith. Whatever the saints have tried to say about faith, it is always about equality. Hinduism has always been about inclusiveness, not exclusion.”About ‘Batwara 1947’In the film, Sunny Deol plays Sikandar Mirza, a man who, after being allotted a house following Partition, discovers a Hindu woman named Mai, played by Shabana Azmi, already living there. articles.title: King Charles and Queen Camilla Make Major Announcement as Harry and Meghan Return to U.K.
articles.summary: It's been a week of big news for the British royal family. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have officially touched back down in the U.K. after six years state...
articles.body:
It's been a week of big news for the British royal family. Prince Harry and Meghan Markle have officially touched back down in the U.K. after six years stateside. And, simultaneously, King Charles and Queen Camilla have announced a major autumn tour across the Caribbean, which will culminate in their attendance at the annual Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

Buckingham Palace announced that the sovereigns would visit the Bahamas, of which King Charles is head of state, followed by Guyana at the invitation of the president and at the request of the U.K. government. This will mark 60 years of diplomacy between the two countries.

The couple will conclude their tour with a stop in Antigua and Barbuda, of which King Charles is also head of state, followed by their participation in the Commonwealth Heads of Government Meeting.

The monarch's major announcement came on the heels of the news that his younger son was relocating back to Britain . The Duke and Duchess of Sussex are reportedly looking at homes in the Cotswolds , with the village of Stow-on-the-Wold seeming to be of particular interest. It would put Prince Harry within two hours of Windsor, where his estranged brother, Prince William , resides with his family.

The decision follows what was reportedly a successful London summer trip, where Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet were reunited with their grandparents for the first time in years. The children are due to be enrolled in a local school for the fall.

articles.title: Brad Paisley gets emotional as he sings Dolly Parton duet solo after her death: ‘Never thought it would be about her’
articles.summary: The country singer said the song has taken on new meaning since Parton’s death on Aug. 25.
articles.body:
Brad Paisley got emotional while paying tribute to late country icon and his former collaborator Dolly Parton.

Two days after Parton's death, Paisley paid tribute to her by performing a solo rendition of their 2005 duet, "When I Get Where I'm Going."

He then choked up while admitting that the song has taken on new meaning since her death.

As the love for Dolly Parton continues pouring in, Brad Paisley paid tribute to the Queen of Country with a bittersweet musical moment.

Days after Parton died at the age of 80 after a " brief battle with cancer ," Paisley surprised the crowd at his Bridgeport, Conn. concert with a raw solo performance of "When I Get Where I'm Going," his 2005 duet featuring Parton. Afterwards, the singer became emotional as he recounted how their collaboration came to be.

"When I recorded that song and sent it to Dolly, I said, 'A couple of people in my life I've lost, and I didn't know if this would relate to you,'" Paisley told the crowd at Hartford HealthCare Amphitheater on Aug. 27. "She immediately said, 'Yes, let me sing on that,' and did."

The song, which explored the idea of life after death, sees Paisley croon the lyrics, "When I get where I'm going, There'll be only happy tears / I will shed the sins and struggles, I have carried all these years / And I'll leave my heart wide open, I will love and have no fear / Yeah when I get where I'm going, Don't cry for me down here."

Paisley, whose voice was thick with emotion as he teared up on stage, went on to say that since Parton's death, the song has begun to resonate in a new way.

"I never thought it would be about her, but it is," he admitted. "It's everything she believed, and we will always love you, Dolly."

On Facebook , the venue shared a clip of Paisley performing the song as a montage of photos — featuring Dolly and a few shots of them together — played on the screen behind him. Among them was a photo of the late country icon smiling, as the text "We Love You Dolly," appeared beneath her.

Parton died on Aug. 25, at the age of 80, following a "brief battle with cancer," her representatives confirmed on Tuesday. In the days since, several stars have paid tribute to her life and legacy, revealing the various ways she influenced their own work or directly offered support. Among those who have honored Parton is Paisley's wife, Kimberly Williams-Paisley , who shared on Instagram that she first met the singer when she recorded her 2005 duet with Paisley.

"She was immediately approachable, funny, kind, and generous," the 54-year-old actress wrote on Instagram . "And her voice! Well, it pierced my soul in the best way, and added so much to an already beautiful song."

Williams-Paisley said that years later, they crossed paths again when she filmed an episode of the Netflix series Dolly Parton's Heartstrings .

"On the day we filmed, there were crazy winds and sideways rain. We were trying to keep a strict schedule and so we soldiered on in the storm. My hair, my wardrobe, my script pages were flying every which way as we got ready to shoot," she recalled. "When Dolly arrived, it was like the storm stopped, but only around her/ She glided across the stage, looking gorgeous and prepared as always, with not ONE HAIR out of place. It must have been the Dolly effect."

Like her husband, she concluded the tribute with a reference to one of Parton's biggest hits: "Dolly will always live on in her music and in our hearts," she wrote. "And we will always love her."

articles.title: Dolly Parton laid to rest in private Nashville funeral, family confirms
articles.summary: Parton was laid to rest Friday in a private Nashville funeral, her great-niece confirmed. Tennessee also moved to rename Nashville's airport in her honor.
articles.body:
Dolly Parton, the beloved "Queen of Country," died Aug. 25 at 80 after "bravely facing a brief battle with cancer," her publicist said .

President Trump ordered U.S. flags flown at half-staff through Sept. 1, while Tennessee Gov. Bill Lee instructed state flags to be lowered, as tributes poured in for one of America's most admired cultural figures.

On Friday, Lee and the Metropolitan Nashville Airport Authority announced they intend to rename Nashville International Airport in Parton's honor. The airport authority will take up the proposal at its Sept. 17 meeting. Parton's team told Lee they were "touched by the idea and open to continuing the conversation," according to a statement from the governor's office.

Parton was laid to rest Friday in a private Nashville funeral, her great-niece Lainey Mae Parton confirmed. She was buried beside her husband, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park, as her family had said would happen.

Here's what we know about plans to remember her.

Parton was buried Friday, Aug. 28, in a small private service for immediate family, in keeping with her wishes. Her great-niece, Lainey Mae Parton, confirmed the news in a tribute posted to Instagram on Saturday. No public memorial has been announced.

Parton told Entertainment Weekly in 2014 that she expected Whitney Houston's cover of her song "I Will Always Love You" to be played.

She also said she wanted the hymn "If We Never Meet Again" to be sung. Parton had long wanted the country-gospel hymn, previously recorded by Elvis Presley, to be part of her funeral, saying that it was her father's favorite.

"It's an old country-gospel church song that talks about, 'If we never meet again this side of heaven, I will meet you on that beautiful shore,'" she said. "That was my daddy's favorite. We did sing it at his funeral, and I would like it to be sung at mine."

She was buried beside her husband of 59 years, Carl Dean, at Woodlawn Memorial Park and Mausoleum in Nashville. The cemetery is also the final resting place of Dean's parents and several country music legends and friends of Parton, including collaborator Porter Wagoner. The cemetery is also the final resting place of Dean's parents and several country music legends and friends of Parton, including collaborator Porter Wagoner.

In the Instagram post announcing her death, Parton's nephew and longtime head of security, Bryan Seaver, detailed her request for a comfortable final resting spot. "Dolly called me and said she wants to rest in a beautiful bed of plush cotton, because after a life of wearing heavy rhinestones, she finally deserves to be comfortable and have some rest," Seaver said.

She is, however, expected to wear her signature high heels, TMZ reported.

While the funeral is set to be private, Parton's official channels are inviting fans to tag @DollyParton on social media and share their memories, or leave a message on her website .

In lieu of flowers, the family has asked that donations be made to Dolly Parton's Imagination Library , the book-gifting program for children she founded in honor of her father.

Several other efforts are also underway to honor the Queen of Country's legacy, including some arranged by Parton herself.

In 2015, Parton left behind a musical time capsule: an unreleased song titled "My Place in History," sealed inside a chestnut "Dream Box" on display at Dollywood's DreamMore Resort.

The box is not scheduled to be opened until Jan. 19, 2046, on what would have been Parton's 100th birthday. She spoke about it publicly over the years, joking to The Kelly Clarkson Show that the wait "bothered" her and that she wished she could dig it up early.

Alongside her musical legacy, Parton's philanthropic projects that she built over many decades will outlive her. A spokesperson confirmed on the day of her death that her Imagination Library program, which has distributed more than 300 million books to children, will continue. "The work ahead has never felt more meaningful, and we will carry it forward as she lifts us all up," the project said.

Dollywood temporarily closed Tuesday to mourn its founder, but plans to continue operating. In an Instagram statement, park president Eugene Naughton said it will carry forward her values of kindness and "dreaming big," adding that her presence remains "alive and well" there.

The Grand Ole Opry, where Parton was a member for nearly 60 years, will dedicate its Saturday night show to her. The sold-out tribute runs at 7 p.m. CT and will be livestreamed on the Opry's Facebook and YouTube channels. Carly Pearce, who began her career at Dollywood, is among the artists set to perform. A portion of ticket sales will go to the Imagination Library.

In Parton's home state of Tennessee, one lawmaker said he would float designating Sept. 25 as "9 to 5 Day," a nod to the title of her hit song. Legislators had proposed erecting a statue of Parton in 2021, but she asked them to withdraw the measure, saying she didn't feel comfortable being "put on a pedestal" while she was still alive, though she left open the possibility later on.

The Nashville International Airport push, first started by fans in a change.org petition in January 2025, gained official backing Friday morning when Lee and airport CEO Doug Kreulen announced the proposal. The petition had passed 160,000 signatures by Friday night.

The name change would make Parton the first woman honored on one of America's 50 busiest airports, according to the Associated Press. However, it is not automatic. The airport authority's current policy requires that people it honors have been dead for at least two years, and its board will address both the policy and Lee's proposal at its Sept. 17 meeting. Nashville Mayor Freddie O'Connell called the idea "wonderful."

Parton's manager, Danny Nozell, said that the singer also greenlit a number of projects before her death, including a biopic, a docuseries, a scripted series, an avatar show, a documentary about her upcoming Broadway musical and an animated series inspired by her children's book Billy the Kid .

Parton's goddaughter, Miley Cyrus, said she might turn to songwriting to process the loss. While the details of their closest moments would remain private, "Dolly would want me to feel it, write a song about it, and then continue on and be strong," she said in a tribute on Instagram.

articles.title: Reading Festival: Messy singer Lola Young makes surprise final day appearance
articles.summary: The singer has been slowly returning to performing after taking a break last year to "work on myself".
articles.body:
Fans at the final day of Reading Festival were treated to a surprise set from singer Lola Young.

"I am backstage, the cat is out of the bag and I am going to be performing so see you... at the Grid stage," she teased on Instagram, before treating fans to hits including number one single Messy and One Thing.

Her performance marks the latest step in a return to the spotlight after she had to cancel a string of shows last year following an on-stage collapse in September.

Young also pulled out of the 2025 Reading festival due to a scheduling clash.

The weekend festival concludes on Sunday with a line-up including performances by drum and bass duo Chase & Status, and Florence + The Machine.

After Charli XCX ushered in her own new era with an electrifying set following her latest release Music, Fashion, Film, Young's return was welcomed by festival-goers in Reading on Sunday.

Young had cancelled her scheduled appearance at Reading Festival last year due to an "unavoidable scheduling conflict".

A month later, Young dropped her microphone, collapsed backwards and had to be helped off stage in front of a festival crowd in New York.

A few days later, she cancelled all shows "for the foreseeable future".

"I really hope you'll give me a second chance once I've had some time to work on myself and come back stronger," she posted in a message to fans at the time.

Young has sought treatment for drug dependency and told the Guardian in 2025 that addiction had dogged her for "a long time".

The pop star has since returned to performing with a small run of shows in the UK, starting with a London gig in March .

"It felt so right being back on stage," she wrote on social media shortly after, but said: "As tempting as it is to jump on a big tour I'm going to continue taking things slowly despite feeling so ready to perform more."

Before touching down in Reading, Young performed at the Electric Picnic Festival in the Republic of Ireland on Saturday.

Although she has returned to performing and released reflective single From Down Here in May this year, fans are still awaiting a fourth album.

Reading Festival winds down on Sunday night with a star-studded cast including indie icon Florence and the Machine, R&B hit-maker Loyle Carner, and Irish rap group Kneecap.

The festival's other site in Leeds, meanwhile, closes after performances from singer-songwriter Raye and multi award-winning rapper Dave on Sunday night.

articles.title: Olivia Rodrigo’s Daisy Chain Fields Festival Was a Day Full of Superstars, Nonprofits, and Joy
articles.summary: On the ground at the inaugural event, which featured artists like Rodrigo, Chappell Roan, Doechii, Sara McLachlan and Stevie Nicks and an inspiring social me...
articles.body:
By the time Olivia Rodrigo hit the stage to headline the inaugural Daisy Chain Fields festival, the sun had set on a sweltering day, and anyone who was fading was sure to feel reenergized both from a welcome breeze and from Rodrigo's set. The superstar had promised special guests, and she delivered, bringing out Lilith Fair founder Sarah McLachlan, whose groundbreaking Nineties fest served as inspiration for Daisy Chain; Alanis Morissette, who stepped in for Karen O after she had a family emergency ; and Stevie Nicks. "I feel like I'm dreaming," Rodrigo told the crowd at Great Park in Irvine, California. "This is the best day of my fuckin' life!"

It certainly felt like the best dream ever for the crowd of mostly women and girls at the festival, which sold out in 30 minutes . The stacked lineup included trailblazers who inspired generations of women to pick up guitars, on-the-rise bands, and pop stars primed to meet the moment. Like Lilith Fair, the all-day celebration was more than just a music festival: It was an inclusive and much-needed gathering — uniting music fans while supporting important causes.

The day before the festival, Rodrigo talked about its philanthropic aims. "It's a real honor to announce that we are donating $10 million to be given directly to these 10 nonprofit partners that you just had the pleasure of hearing about," Rodrigo said at a press conference attended by 10 organizations that advocate for women and girls and were participating in the festival.

Those nonprofit participants included Baby2Baby , which provides children in need with basic necessities; Black Mamas Matter Alliance (BMMA), which advocates for Black mothers' rights and provides resources throughout and after pregnancy; Center for Reproductive Rights , a legal organization that advocates for reproductive rights and health care access for women worldwide; FreeFrom , which works to end gender-based violence by providing survivors with financial resources and more; Jhpiego , which provides critical health care to women and families worldwide; John Hopkins Center for Indigenous Health , which advances health equity for Indigenous communities worldwide; National Domestic Workers Alliance , which advocates for the rights of domestic workers; National Institute for Reproductive Health , which works to advance reproductive health care for all at the state and local level; National Women's Law Center , which fights for gender justice on the legal front and beyond; and Planned Parenthood , which works to protect, provide, and expand access to sexual and reproductive health care and education. Net proceeds from the event are being directed to Daisy Chain Fields Fund, which benefits those nonprofits.

When describing the way music, community, and action were joining together at Daisy Chain, one word came up regularly at the press conference: "joy." And that feeling was palpable throughout the grounds on Saturday.

Lines formed outside of Daisy Chain Reaction, the area where the nonprofits invited attendees to learn about their organizations while participating in crafts like assembling daisy chains and making flower crowns. Several fans, many dressed in Rodrigo-style baby doll dresses, said they were drawn to the event because of their love of the superstar, but also because they want a better world for women and girls. Alannie, 18, says that at her age, the ticket price was a big investment, but after learning Rodrigo's motive behind the fest, she wanted to participate. "I see it as a purpose, to give my money to all these foundations," she says.

A trio of early-thirties Filipina women — Nerissa, Christabel, and Monica — were also excited to support the nonprofits. "I very strongly resonate with the different organizations she was promoting," Nerissa says, adding that she's used Planned Parenthood's services in the past. Christabel adds, "I think it's such a beautiful thing that Olivia is creating a festival and a place for us all to gather to really empower, advance, and advocate for women and the organizations at Daisy Chain Reaction." Monica addressed the issue of representation, saying, "[Olivia] is Filipino, so she's representing our people, and also the lineup of amazing artists that she put together."

That lineup made for 14 sets and 10 hours of great music. Things kicked off with Quiet Light, the stage name of singer-medical student Riya Mahesh. She and her dancers slowly grooved, striking ballerina-style moves during "Postinternefame" from her 2026 mixtape Blue Angel Sparkling Silver 2 . Eli Miller, who performs under her first name, followed. Amid songs like "Nobody's Girl" and "Girl of Your Dreams," Eli delivered a powerful message about loving our neighbors, "no matter what they believe or don't." She also pledged money to some of the day's participating organizations.

"It's fucking hot right now," Rachel Chinouriri told the audience during her set. "The U.K. ain't like this." But Chinouriri kept the vibe going anyway, tearing through her tender 2025 single " Can We Talk About Isaac " while premiering material from her upcoming album I Think I Spoke Too Soon, "It's about my twenties, and realizing I'm not the person I thought I was," she said of the album. "And I can become whoever I want to be."

Following her performance, Chinouriri said she was excited to join the lineup, shouted out Lilith Fair, and gave kudos to Rodrigo for her inclusiveness when it came to the nonprofit partners. BMMA in particular is close to her heart. "It's really heartwarming to see [Rodrigo] take the initiative for that because sometimes Black women are very overlooked in many ways or not understood, especially in health care," she tells Rolling Stone . "I think that the level of thoughtfulness of that was so sweet."

Devon Again got the call to join the festival just last Thursday, after Katseye had to cancel due to member Megan Skiendiel's ankle injury. "I said, 'Duh bitch, obviously I wanna do it," she told the crowd. But Eyekons got a taste of Katseye's Lara Raj, Yoonchae Jeung, and Skiendiel, who appeared at the start of Devon's set to introduce nonprofit Baby2Baby. Afterward, Devon performed a country-tinged set, which included fan favorites "Skittles" and "Cherry Cola."

Die Spitz took the prize for calisthenics at Daisy Chain. The four-piece from Austin, Texas ripped through their midday set, where the blazing sun was no match for their energy (if a little hard on their face paint). At one point bassist Kate Halter did a full-on handstand. Die Spitz's all-girl metal was met warmly, so much so that singer ​​Eleanor Livingston jumped into the crowd to join the revelers.

Back in 2022, Santigold took a hiatus from the road, telling Rolling Stone about the "cultural crisis" and economic and mental-health challenges plaguing those who make music for a living. She resumed touring in 2024, though the dates have been selective and for short runs, which makes any chance to see her live special. Her Daisy Chain set was thoroughly joyful, including a dance contest and a bevy of fan-favorites like "L.E.S. Artistes," "Lights Out," and "Disparate Youth."

Feminist-punk trailblazers Bikini Kill, meanwhile, had taken a couple decades off, but came back hard for a reunion tour in 2019. They've barely slowed down since. "What a gift Olivia has given all of us to have this festival," singer Kathleen Hanna told the crowd. Like many of the bands here, Bikini Kill used their limited stage time to play the hits. Though they blazed through two songs from their last album, 1996's Reject All American , the band focused mostly on early songs, opening with "Double Dare Ya" from their 1992 EP, before sliding into "This Is Not a Test."

When Hanna told a story about a 40-year-old man creeping on her when she was 17 to introduce the track "Feels Blind," the crowd was rapt — "This is the most engaged crowd I've ever seen in my life," she said. Closing with "Suck My Left One" and "Rebel Girl," Hanna growled and danced her way across the stage, reminding the audience exactly why this band influenced a generation of women — and were integral to a festival like this ever coming into existence.

Mitski was feeling the communal spirit during her set in the late afternoon, telling the audience multiple times that she loved "every one of you." She had already put that love into practice with a series of PSAs concerning the extreme heat: advising fans to sit down right where you are if you're faint, head to the pit if you need water, and wear sunscreen. Of course, Mitski also delivered a stellar set, which included highlights from her 2026 album Nothing's About to Happen to Me like "Where's My Phone?" and "That White Cat," alongside fan-favorites like "Nobody." "I feel like we should do this every year," she said to loud cheers. "For the rest of our lives you can be like, 'Oh yeah, I'm OG DCF.'"

The Breeders have been in the Rodrigo camp for a few years now, opening up for the pop star on several dates of her GUTS tour. But their inclusion in the festival was part of the appeal of the lineup — the incredible mix of old and new. The fact that singer Kim Deal took the stage wearing a Shirley Chisholm shirt — referencing the first Black woman to serve in Congress — made their set feel all the more connected to the past. Starting their set with 1994's "Drivin' on 9," the band included other OG-era classics like "Do You Love Me Now?" and "Cannonball," while working in new, unreleased songs like "Alien Eyes," which they've been playing throughout their summer tour. Getting to test things out on the road, Deal told Paste magazine, is "like it was back in the old days."

When Doechii hit Lollapalooza in 2025 , she stole the show as headmaster of the school of hip-hop. At Daisy Chain, she signaled a new era, one that is pink-hued and incorporates all the right moves onstage. Wearing a bikini while covered in hot-pink body makeup, she and her equally pink-painted dancers delivered incredible choreography on a headlining-worthy stage setup, complete with a large riser, an LED screen and metal bars that Doechii at one point acrobatically flipped over. She had us from the jump, launching into "ExtraL," her 2025 collab with Jennie. Other collab tracks — the SZA team-up "Girl Get Up" and "Swamp Bitches," with Rico Nasty — hit hard, even if those artists weren't present Saturday. Doechii's mashups also landed: "Anxiety" sampled Gotye's "Somebody That I Used to Know," and Doechii freestyled over Beyoncé's "America Has a Problem," and even wove Britney Spears' "Toxic" into the mix. She ended one of the best performances of the day with a rousing version of "Denial Is a River," an instant-classic from 2024's Alligator Bites Never Heal .

Garbage's set was plagued by technical difficulties, but singer Shirley Manson kept her cool, joking that this was just the kind of thing the band was used to. "An entire career made up of this kind of carry on," she joked in her Scottish brogue. This, she said, was a lesson to the younger folks in the crowd: Even when things don't go the way you'd hoped, the world keeps spinning. "You don't have to be perfect," she said. "You can fuck up."

Despite the hurdles, the band delivered 1990s classics like "Only Happy When It Rains," "When I Grow Up," and "Stupid Girl" (which slipped into a brief cover of Bikini Kill's "Rebel Girl," much to the crowd's delight), as well as newer tracks like "There's No Future in Optimism" and "Chinese Fire Hose," off last year's Let All That We Imagine Be the Light .

Manson took breaks to address the audience, praising Rodrigo's ability to bring the multigenerational crowd together. "We've been around since before most of you were born," she said. "So to be included in this festival lineup is an immense privilege, and it's not one we take lightly." She also imparted some words of hope for these dark times. "I just want to assure you all — because I just turned 60, so I'm very old," she joked. "But if you just keep putting one foot in front of the other as you move through your life, I can guarantee you, it's like putting pennies in a bank. Sooner or later, you build the life that you want."

At the end of last year, Chappell Roan spoke about what she envisioned for 2026. She said it will be "the year of taking care of myself and others and really engaging in a community that feels real and not online. Volunteering locally and giving money to organizations I believe in." Daisy Chain was the perfect place for that, and the crowd erupted when Roan emerged onstage around 7 p.m., wearing a lavender set and matching boots.

Though the sweltering day had cooled down by then, "Hot to Go!" still felt incredibly fitting. Roan tore through other favorites off her 2023 smash debut The Rise and Fall of a Midwest Princess , including "Red Wine Supernova," "Pink Pony Club," and "Casual," plus the gem " Good Luck, Babe! " and her most recent single " The Subway ." When Roan appeared on the October, 2024 cover of Rolling Stone , Rodrigo spoke to us about the superstar. "I remember her walking into the studio one day and just flat-out saying 'I don't give a fuck about what people say anymore. If I like it, then it's good,'" Rodrigo said. "I could tell she actually meant it, too. That's her magic."

María Zardoya recorded the debut album for her solo project, Not for Radio , in a house in Upstate New York in the middle of winter, surrounded by snow and ice. The Daisy Chain locale could not have been more different. But Zardoya , best known as the singer of the Marias, brought a chill over the audience with a handful of tracks from Melt and her new EP, Bloom . Maybe it was the woodland-themed set over which she seemed to float, or the bittersweet subject matter — the project is partially inspired by a split from the Marias' drummer, Zardoya's longtime partner — or maybe it was just the fact that the sun finally went down, but Zardoya's set offered a moment of catharsis. With songs like "Puddle," "Swan," and "My Turn," she reminded the crowd that it's OK to be a little down sometimes, too.

Then it was time for Rodrigo, who capped off the night with a set that, appropriately, featured McLachlan. The pair performed McLachlan's 1997 hit "Building a Mystery," and dedicated "Angel" to Dolly Parton, who died on Aug. 25. They also treated the crowd to the live debut of Rodrigo's recent single " Serena Joy ."

Rodrigo next teamed up with Morissette — with whom she appeared on the cover of Rolling Stone in 2021 — for a scorching version of Morissette's classic "Ironic." Philanthropist Melinda French Gates joined Rodrigo and pledged to double the $10 million being donated. Rodrigo's final guest was Nicks. Together they performed a showstopping " Landslide ," which found the pair trading verses and dancing together. "She reminds me of me, when I was her age a hundred years ago," Nicks said of Rodrigo. "And I'm somewhat awestruck that she could do all this. Because it's so hard — you have no idea — putting this together with all of these people. And she's done it, with this grace." There were also plenty of Rodrigo's own classics, including "Bad Idea Right?," "Good 4 U," and " Drivers License ," the hit that first gave us a peek of the superstar she became, each drawing field-wide singalongs.

When Rodrigo announced Daisy Chain Fields, expectations were high, as fans hoped for a festival that delivered onstage and meet its mission for empowering women and girls. Saturday exceeded those expectations. And it turned out that Mitski may have been onto something when she suggested we do this again: "See you next year!" Rodrigo exclaimed at the end of her performance.

articles.title: Banbury Early Music Festival 'proud' of international award nomination
articles.summary: Oxfordshire festival says it is "a remarkable milestone" for an event established three years ago.
articles.body:
An Oxfordshire festival dedicated to medieval, renaissance and baroque music has been nominated for an international award.

The Banbury Early Music Festival said its nomination for Audience Project of the Year at the REMA Awards 2026 represented "a remarkable milestone for a festival established only three years ago".

This year's festival will take place on 26 and 27 September across the town centre before the team travels to Bruges, Belgium, for the awards ceremony on 25 November.

The festival directors said that while early music "can sometimes be perceived as something specialist or inaccessible" they had always "wanted to break down that barrier".

The REMA awards celebrate innovative and impactful projects shaping the early music sector in Europe and beyond.

European early music covers the period between 1250 and 1750, particularly when performed using musical instruments from the time, such as the lute, crumhorn and baroque violin.

The Banbury festival was established in 2023 by early musicians Dylan McCaig, Heidi Fardell and Alison Kinder, and has been bringing leading professional musicians together with amateur performers, young musicians, instrument makers, local organisations and audiences.

The nomination means it will represent the UK on the European stage alongside Team Recorder, a project created by recorder player, educator and YouTube personality Sarah Jeffery.

The directors said they were "enormously proud" seeing the festival on the international shortlist.

They said in a statement: "From the beginning, we wanted to create something firmly rooted in Banbury but ambitious enough to attract outstanding musicians and audiences from across the country.

"We strongly believe that people should not have to travel to a major city to experience world class music and culture."

They added that the mixture of renowned artists, local musicians, school pupils, amateurs and complete newcomers who took part in the festival made it "so exciting".

The nomination belongs "just as much to our audiences, volunteers, musicians, workshop participants, supporters and the wider Banbury community as it does to us", said the directors.

articles.title: Professor Murder Rides the Subway is a forgotten slice of dance punk perfection
articles.summary: Professor Murder Rides the Subway is the sound of mid-aughts Brooklyn in audio form.
articles.body: I recently dug out my CDs and started reripping them all. I’ve found a few forgotten gems in there, but few hit harder for me than the beautifully concise Professor Murder Rides the Subway EP. There was a period of time in the mid-aughts in NYC where it seemed like every indie band wanted you to let loose, dance like no one was watching, and just have some damn fun. Few embodied that as much as New York dance punk band Professor Murder. LCD Soundsystem and The Rapture were the biggest names of the dance punk revival. But there were also bands like Rahim, Liars, Dan Deacon, and countless lesser-known acts on DFA that you could see on any given weekend around NYC. And I spent a lot of time in those venues, shamelessly dancing my ass off to all of them. [Media: There’s something about Professor Murder’s specific blend of cheap synth blasts, shouted vocal chants, busy syncopated percussion, and throbbing bass that perfectly captures the vibe of the NYC music scene circa 2006. At their heart, the tracks on the 16-minute EP are built around a simple disco stomp (save for the brief a cappella of “Pedigree”). They’re dressed up with cowbell and other tuned percussion elements to add complexity. But they’re never allowed to disrupt the groove. While some of their contemporaries like LCD Soundsystem were chasing bigger, more melodic textures, Professor Murder trafficked in stripped-back arrangements where, arguably, the drums are the lead instrument. While there are hooks and melodies to grab on to, like the fuzzy bass on “Camron’s New Color (Part 3)”, they’re always a little quieter in the mix. The EP is bookended with two songs that are basically the Platonic ideal of 2000’s dance punk: “Champion” and “Free Stress Test.” If there was any justice in the world, the latter would have catapulted the band to at least Rapture levels of success. I dare you to not at least nod your head along to the beat. Professor Murder Rides the Subway is available on Bandcamp and most major streaming services, including Apple Music, YouTube Music, Spotify, Deezer, and Qobuz.

Ney Matogrosso posa para o fotógrafo norte-americano David LaChapelle em ensaio no Jardim Botânico da cidade de São Paulo (SP) — Foto: David LaChapelle / Divulgação

♬ Não foi surpresa quando a turnê que Ney Matogrosso fará por estádios e arenas do Brasil ao longo de 2027, “85 anos de ousadia” , foi anunciada oficialmente à imprensa na última quarta-feira, 26 de agosto. Afinal, a notícia da turnê já tinha sido dada extraoficialmente pelo jornalista Julio Maria, biógrafo do cantor.

A maior novidade foi a divulgação das imagens feitas para apresentar a turnê que estreia em São Paulo (SP) em 30 de janeiro no estádio Nubank Parque. É que as imagens de Ney produzidas pelo fotógrafo norte-americano David LaChappelle são um espetáculo à parte.

Captadas em ensaio realizado no Jardim Botânico da cidade de São Paulo (SP), as imagens retratam Ney em cores vivas – uma das características das fotos de David LaChappelle, aclamado pela criação de imagens em cores vibrantes e em cenários suntuosos, com mix de referências da arte clássica barroca e da PopArt do mestre Andy Warhol (1928 – 1987).

Contudo, mais do que o colorido que atrai instantaneamente atenções e olhares, as imagens parecem captar a íntima relação de Ney Matogrosso com a natureza. Ney é um bicho-homem que sempre se afinou com os animais. Há um amor genuíno do artista por bichos, plantas, pedras e rios.

Tudo isso está nas fotografias feitas por David LaChappelle para divulgar a turnê “85 anos de ousadia” . As imagens em si já são um espetáculo!

articles.body:
Marco e Mário fazem o show oficial de retorno no Camaru 2026 — Foto: Divulgação

Uberlândia completa 138 anos nesta segunda-feira, 31 de agosto. No aniversário da cidade, 62ª edição do Camaru - Exposição Agropecuária de Uberlândia, tem entrada gratuita para a população. O grande show da noite marco o retorno da dupla Marco e Mário aos palcos. O festival 'Uai Sô' , que começa às 12h, entre outras atrações, tem show de Renato Teixeira.

A Prefeitura de Uberlândia também leva vários serviços para o parque dentro do projeto Uberlândia Viva. Confira a programação e horários desta segunda-feira abaixo.

O Sindicato Rural de Uberlândia informou que será possível adquirir ingressos para o Espaço Varanda em todos os dias de programação gratuita. As vendas são feitas pelo site do Camaru ou na bilheteria do Parque de Exposições.

Nesta segunda-feira também será iniciada a programação da Cozinha Show, no Espaço do Produtor, e o tema do dia é a Produção Artesanal do Doce de Leite.

Formada em Uberlândia há mais de duas décadas, a dupla Marco e Mário retorna ao Camaru em um show marcado pela conexão com a cidade onde a carreira começou.

Para os irmãos, a apresentação durante as comemorações do aniversário do município representa a oportunidade de reviver momentos importantes ao lado do público que acompanhou a trajetória da dupla desde os primeiros passos.

Ao longo da carreira, Marco e Mário conquistaram projeção nacional com músicas que integraram trilhas sonoras de novelas e se tornaram sucessos do sertanejo. Entre os principais hits estão 'A Mulher Mais Feliz', 'Quem é Ela', 'Uma Chance' a 'Mais' e 'Flecha do Cupido'.

articles.title: A música de IA que plagiou Taylor Swift, viralizou nas redes e agora não para de tocar nas rádios brasileiras | G1
articles.standfirst: 'A Sina de Ofélia', inspirada em hit da popstar, clona as vozes de Dilsinho e Luísa Sonza e já foi reproduzidas milhares de vezes no rádio, o que pode configurar um crime.
articles.summary: 'A Sina de Ofélia', inspirada em hit da popstar, clona as vozes de Dilsinho e Luísa Sonza e já foi reproduzidas milhares de vezes no rádio, o que pode configurar um crime.
articles.body:
Luísa Sonza, à esquerda, teve sua voz clonada por inteligência artificial para cantar em português o hit The Fate of Ophelia, de Taylor Swift — Foto: BBC

Ao escutar A Sina de Ofélia , é fácil reconhecer a voz de Luísa Sonza . Logo depois, surge Dilsinho. A popstar e o pagodeiro fazem um dueto improvável, mas convincente. Até você descobrir que nenhum deles cantou essa música de verdade.

A Sina de Ofélia foi produzida com inteligência artificial generativa. Clonaram as vozes dos artistas brasileiros e os puseram para cantar uma tradução para o português de uma música que, na verdade, é de Taylor Swift ( The Fate of Ophelia ).

Só falta descobrir quem fez tudo isso. A faixa acumula milhões de reproduções nas plataformas de streaming e nas redes sociais , mas sua autoria segue desconhecida — o que é comum no caso de conteúdos feitos com IA.

A Sina de Ofélia foi compartilhada à exaustão no Spotify , Instagram e TikTok. O que quase ninguém parece ter percebido — inclusive os próprios artistas — é que, enquanto fazia sucesso na internet , ela também começava a tocar nas rádios brasileiras, principalmente nas emissoras do interior do país.

Um relatório da Crowley, empresa de monitoramento e auditoria de rádio, feito a pedido da BBC News Brasil, mostra que a música foi executada 3.064 vezes em 47 estações de rádio.

Mas esse número pode ser ainda maior, visto que a Crowley monitora apenas regiões selecionadas, concentradas nos principais mercados publicitários do país — a região Norte, por exemplo, fica de fora. Além disso, o levantamento considera somente as execuções de segunda a sexta-feira, das 7h às 19h.

Ainda assim, não é pouca coisa. A Sina de Ofélia registrou, em alguns meses, um volume de execuções próximo ao que a música mais tocada do país costuma alcançar em uma semana nas estimativas da Crowley.

Além disso, na maioria dos casos, uma exposição desse tamanho é resultado de investimentos maciços de artistas e gravadoras em publicidade nas rádios — o famoso jabá —, enquanto A Sina de Ofélia alcançou esse volume sem que tenha sido identificado qualquer tipo de financiamento.

As execuções, de toda forma, geraram ao menos R$ 50 mil em lucros, segundo o Escritório Central de Arrecadação e Distribuição, o Ecad, responsável por arrecadar e distribuir os direitos autorais de execuções públicas de músicas no Brasil — no rádio, na televisão , na internet, em eventos como o Carnaval ou na sonorização de espaços públicos como shopping centers .

O dinheiro está retido. O Ecad informou à reportagem que ainda não sabe o que fazer com os valores arrecadados, já que, em tese, não há um autor a quem os R$ 5 mil possam ser repassados.

É possível que, em algum momento, o valor seja redistribuído entre artistas cadastrados na instituição e que atualmente estejam em rotação nas rádios — o que renderia não mais do que algumas dezenas de reais para cada.

Avatar de Luísa Sonza criado com IA para o clipe de A Sina de Ofélia, que circula nas redes sociais e no YouTube — Foto: Reprodução

Segundo especialistas ouvidos pela BBC, A Sina de Ofélia pode ser considerada uma fraude, e sua reprodução nas rádios pode configurar crime.

Caso seja descoberto e processado, seu autor pode sofrer sanções civis — como indenização ligadas a perdas financeiras e a danos à imagem dos artistas — e criminais — que podem incluir pena de prisão de até três anos.

As emissoras que estão tocando a música também podem ser punidas, segundo o advogado Guilherme Valente, especialista em direito autoral pela Organização Mundial da Propriedade Intelectual.

"No rádio, existe curadoria, então há uma responsabilidade maior, porque alguém está escolhendo as músicas que vão ao ar, diferentemente de uma plataforma de conteúdo criado pelo usuário, como os aplicativos de streaming , em que qualquer um pode compartilhar uma música. O grau de responsabilidade é diferente", ele diz.

A reportagem procurou os artistas que foram alvo dessa fraude — Luísa Sonza e Dilsinho, por terem suas vozes clonadas, e Taylor Swift , por ter sua composição e melodia copiadas.

Informalmente, as equipes de Sonza e Dilsinho disseram estar surpresas e afirmaram que nem sequer sabiam que isso estava acontecendo. A faixa, afinal, não está tocando nos grandes centros onde ficam seus escritórios, como São Paulo e Rio de Janeiro .

Nenhum dos dois, porém, respondeu aos questionamentos da reportagem ou quis gravar entrevista.

A BBC também procurou a Sony Music, gravadora que representa Sonza; a Som Livre, responsável por Dilsinho; e a Universal Music, que representa Swift no Brasil e nos Estados Unidos . Nenhuma das empresas respondeu.

A reportagem também não obteve resposta da rádio que mais reproduziu A Sina de Ofélia , segundo o relatório da Crowley: a Mega FM, de Ribeirão Preto, no interior paulista.

Para a superintendente do Ecad, Isabel Amorim, A Sina de Ofélia é apenas "a ponta do iceberg " do avanço da IA generativa na indústria musical.

Com poucos cliques, vale lembrar, é possível transformar em música até um texto sem qualquer sonoridade, escolhendo detalhes como o gênero da canção, a velocidade e outros elementos sonoros.

A avaliação de Amorim encontra respaldo nos dados da Deezer, uma das maiores plataformas de streaming musical e, até o momento, a única a divulgar um relatório sobre a presença da IA generativa em seu acervo.

Segundo a empresa, metade das faixas adicionadas diariamente à plataforma é gerada por IA. O fenômeno atingiu seu pico em junho, quando mais de 45 mil dos 90 mil cadastros realizados correspondiam a músicas desse tipo.

As demais plataformas não divulgam dados semelhantes, o que impede uma comparação mais ampla. Mas os números da Deezer servem como termômetro, já que a maioria das canções são cadastradas simultaneamente em diferentes serviços de streaming — há empresas pagas para fazer essa distribuição, aliás.

Os dados da Deezer retratam um cenário global, mas os números do Ecad ajudam a dimensionar o fenômeno no Brasil.

Entre janeiro e agosto, 62.292 músicas criadas com IA tiveram seus royalties retidos pela instituição, entre elas a faixa que plagiou uma música de Taylor Swift .

A maior parte das retenções ocorreu por reproduções em streaming , categoria que inclui as redes sociais, como mostra o gráfico abaixo. Mas as rádios também aparecem nesse cenário, respondendo por 5% dos valores retidos.

A Associação Brasileira de Emissoras de Rádio e Televisão (Abert), que representa cerca de 3.000 emissoras no país, diz não interferir na programação de seus associados, mas afirma orientá-los a não reproduzir músicas feitas por IA.

Rodolfo Salema, diretor de assuntos jurídicos e regulatórios da entidade, avalia que o caso de A Sina de Ofélia parece isolado e que não há outras músicas do tipo sendo executadas pelas rádios.

"É algo excepcional, porque a música explodiu e o pessoal ficou meio cego", diz. "Pode ser demanda da audiência, porque a rádio tem até hoje muito pedido de música, e às vezes tem um desconhecimento do pessoal da programação sobre uma discussão maior sobre IA."

A Sina de Ofélia , porém, não está nem entre as músicas com os maiores valores retidos pelo Ecad. As três que aparecem no topo da lista, segundo a instituição, são Comida Feliz , voltada ao público infantil, com o refrão "vamos comer para ficarmos fortes e crescer"; Criando Memórias , sobre afetos e momentos simples da vida; e Um Novo Ser , sobre fé e busca por Deus .

A faixa gospel, aliás, é a única das três que as plataformas de streaming sinalizam como conteúdo gerado por IA e que tem algum crédito de autoria: Hikari de Jesus. O nome, porém, pertence a um personagem que também foi criado por IA, cuja autoria é desconhecida.

Hikari de Jesus é um personagem de IA que faz sucesso cantando músicas gospel cujas letras e melodias também são criadas com a tecnologia — Foto: Reprodução

Embora nenhuma dessas três músicas copie uma faixa específica, como A Sina de Ofélia , o Ecad questiona a forma como elas foram criadas.

Segundo a instituição, a IA usada para escrever as letras e transformá-las em música se vale de uma grande biblioteca de obras feitas por humanos, que estaria sendo apropriada pelos serviços de IA sem autorização. Por isso, entende que também há uma infração de direitos autorais nesses casos.

"Um músico usa a mixagem para fazer algum arranjo. Isso é natural, como um fotógrafo ajustar a luz da foto com tecnologia. Mas é diferente de não criar nada e copiar o trabalho dos outros", diz Amorim, do Ecad. "Não podem pegar um trabalho dos criadores, colocar num sistema, treinar a máquina e achar que está tudo certo."

A discussão sobre os limites desse uso da IA ainda está em curso, e há um projeto de lei sobre o tema em tramitação no Congresso brasileiro.

Na falta de definições concretas, porém, o Ecad vem acumulando vitórias na Justiça contra estabelecimentos que criaram rádios internas com músicas feitas com IA e alegavam não precisar pagar direitos autorais.

O caso mais emblemático, porém, não chegou ao Judiciário. Foi o da loja de brinquedos Ri Happy, que inicialmente afirmou que deixaria de pagar direitos autorais ao Ecad por usar músicas feitas por inteligência artificial em sua rádio interna, mas depois voltou atrás, conta Amorim.

"A Ri Happy passou por um momento de pensar: 'Ah, não vou pagar porque estou fazendo minhas próprias músicas'. Mas depois repensaram: 'Não, eu preciso continuar contribuindo para a música, para a cultura brasileira, para o trabalho do criador'. O que a gente tem feito é um trabalho muito de conscientização", diz a porta-voz do Ecad.

As duas Ofélias — e no que consiste um plágio

No caso de A Sina de Ofélia , não estamos diante de uma inspiração difusa em uma grande biblioteca de músicas produzidas por seres humanos ao longo da história, mas de elementos que permitem uma comparação direta com a fonte original.

Além do título e da protagonista — inspirada em Hamlet , de William Shakespeare —, a música mantém a mesma estrutura narrativa e reproduz diversas imagens e ideias de The Fate of Ophelia .

Logo no início, as duas faixas trazem o eu lírico dizendo que foi chamado por um megafone e associando o interlocutor ao fogo.

Depois, as letras chegam à mesma imagem de uma mulher isolada em uma torre, antes de ser resgatada por seu amor.

No refrão, ambas afirmam que esse encontro a salvou da "sina" — ou do "destino" — de Ofélia, que, na obra do dramaturgo inglês, é a morte.

Outras imagens também são preservadas na versão brasileira, como a de se afogar na tristeza e a descrição do amor como uma "cama fria cheia de escorpiões", em inglês, e "um ninho de escorpiões", em português.

Há algumas mudanças. O verso " pledge allegiance to your hands ", por exemplo, poderia ser traduzido ao pé da letra como "juro lealdade às suas mãos", mas ganhou contornos mais coloquiais e virou "tô fechada com você, não vou voltar".

Ainda assim, a sequência é a mesma: solidão, chegada do parceiro e resgate. Essa proximidade faz com que A Sina de Ofélia se pareça menos com uma música inspirada na composição de Taylor Swift e mais com uma tradução dela, segundo especialistas ouvidos pela reportagem.

Essa é uma discussão central para diferenciar o que seria uma inspiração do que poderia ser considerado plágio — e, portanto, um crime —, afirma o advogado Guilherme Valente, que também integra a Comissão de Direito das Artes da Ordem dos Advogados do Brasil (OAB) em São Paulo.

"Qualquer um pode escrever uma música inspirada na história de Ofélia. Isso não é proibido, até porque a obra já caiu em domínio público. A questão é o grau de similaridade", diz.

Ele explica que o direito autoral não protege uma ideia, mas a forma como ela é expressa. "A ideia não é exclusiva. O que é exclusivo é como se conta essa ideia, a visão que o autor tem dela e como ele coloca tudo no papel."

Isso vale para qualquer produção artística — um filme , um livro ou uma música, embora cada linguagem tenha suas especificidades. O mesmo vale para traduções, acrescenta o especialista.

"A tradução é uma obra derivada, só que, para traduzir uma obra, é preciso ter autorização do autor. Um dos direitos autorais é justamente a exclusividade para adaptar a obra de outras formas — e a tradução é uma adaptação."

Por que a música continua tocando se pode ser um plágio?

Essa é uma pergunta difícil de responder, mas, em linhas gerais, isso se deve ao fato de que os artistas envolvidos — tanto Luísa Sonza e Dilsinho quanto Taylor Swift — não procuraram fazer valer seus direitos.

Pelo contrário: os artistas brasileiros chegaram a se engajar com a música e fizeram vídeos para as redes sociais usando-a como trilha sonora.

Sonza publicou um vídeo dublando a canção, que já ultrapassou 1 milhão de visualizações e reúne 900 mil curtidas, além de ter participado de um vídeo de uma influenciadora dançando a música. Dilsinho também dublou a canção e escreveu no vídeo: "Ué, já lançou?".

Os artistas não responderam à BBC por que decidiram apoiar um conteúdo que pode ser fruto de plágio.

Profissionais da indústria que conversaram com a reportagem em caráter reservado, porém, afirmam que só os custos com advogados para enviar uma notificação extrajudicial a uma emissora de rádio, pedindo que pare de tocar a música, ou a uma plataforma de streaming , solicitando a remoção da faixa de seu catálogo, já são maiores do que o prejuízo financeiro que os artistas possam estar tendo.

Vale lembrar que, embora a canção tenha viralizado na internet e já tenha sido tocada milhares de vezes nas rádios, o Ecad registrou R$ 50 mil em direitos autorais gerados pela faixa — uma cifra ínfima para artistas desse porte.

Além disso, acrescentam os profissionais do setor, os artistas podem até transformar o pequeno prejuízo em oportunidade, aproveitando o sucesso da música para promover sua imagem e, por que não, sua voz, no caso das reproduções nas rádios.

Mas há também um certo limbo na legislação brasileira que é relevante para essa discussão.

Duas leis podem ter impacto sobre o setor: o Marco Civil da Internet, que regula as plataformas de streaming e foi criado em 2014, quase uma década antes da popularização da inteligência artificial generativa; e a Lei de Direitos Autorais, criada em 1998, muito antes não só da IA, mas da própria ideia de streaming .

"O Marco Civil da Internet criou essa regra que a gente chama de safe harbor principle , o princípio do porto seguro. Isso significa que a responsabilidade da plataforma só surge a partir do momento em que há uma decisão judicial mandando remover aquele conteúdo", explica o advogado Guilherme Valente.

"A gente até tem decisões judiciais que dizem que a plataforma é responsável antes de uma decisão judicial, mas precisa ter ao menos uma notificação do titular dos direitos, avisando que há uma violação."

Taylor Swift em show em Londres durante sua última turnê, a The Eras, em agosto de 2024 — Foto: Gareth Cattermole/TAS24/Getty Images for TAS Rights Management/Via BBC

A avaliação do advogado Guilherme Valente — de que os aplicativos não precisam agir antes que um artista reclame seus direitos — é corroborada pelas próprias empresas de streaming .

Procurado pela BBC News Brasil, o Spotify, plataforma de música mais usada no país, não respondeu especificamente sobre A Sina de Ofélia . Em suas diretrizes, porém, a empresa afirma que não consegue determinar sozinha se houve uma infração.

"O Spotify não sabe se o uso da voz de outro artista é um trecho devidamente licenciado ou uma colaboração; portanto, precisamos receber uma reivindicação do artista para saber que a imitação não é autorizada."

A Deezer, outra líder de mercado, também reiterou que precisa de uma "notificação formal" para tomar providências, mas acrescentou que A Sina de Ofélia foi identificada como conteúdo gerado por IA e recebeu um selo.

Segundo a empresa, músicas que recebem essa sinalização ficam fora das recomendações da plataforma, tanto nas playlists editoriais oficiais quanto nas sugestões feitas pelos algoritmos com base no perfil dos usuários.

No YouTube, a regra é semelhante. Após a BBC enviar sete clipes para análise, um deles saiu do ar, enquanto os demais receberam o selo de conteúdo gerado por IA.

Questionada sobre o motivo da remoção, a empresa, que pertence ao Google, afirmou que o canal ao qual o vídeo pertencia havia infringido suas políticas de uso, mas não especificou qual regra havia sido violada.

TikTok e Meta — dona do Facebook e do Instagram — também disseram que podem remover conteúdos após denúncias. A empresa acrescentou que a publicação contínua de material que desrespeita direitos autorais pode levar à desativação da conta do infrator.
